groups.title: The Event Loop In Depth
groups.question: Walk through what really happens inside the Node.js event loop when your server handles a request.

followUps.libuv & the Thread Pool: What kinds of work go to the libuv thread pool, and what happens when that pool is saturated?
followUps.process.nextTick vs setImmediate: Why can recursive process.nextTick calls make a server look frozen?

evidence.text: Some work, like file system calls, DNS lookups, crypto and compression, runs on libuv's thread pool instead of the main JavaScript thread.
The pool is small by default (4 threads), so when it's full, new tasks queue up and even unrelated file or crypto work gets slow.
Most network I/O doesn't use the pool; the operating system handles it asynchronously.

notEnough: Only saying libuv handles async work without saying what goes to the pool or what happens when it's full.

misconceptions.text: Says every async operation, including all network requests, runs on the thread pool.

evidence.text: process.nextTick callbacks run right after the current operation, before the event loop moves on to I/O or timers.
setImmediate callbacks run in the check phase of the next loop iteration, after I/O has had its turn.
Recursive nextTick calls keep the loop from ever reaching I/O, so the server stops answering requests.

notEnough: Only saying nextTick runs sooner than setImmediate without explaining why recursion freezes the server.

groups.title: Core Modules
groups.question: Explain how you use Node.js core modules for files and events without hurting server performance.

followUps.The fs Module & Async I/O: Why is calling fs.readFileSync inside a request handler a problem under load?
followUps.EventEmitter Pattern: How can forgetting to remove EventEmitter listeners cause a slow memory leak?

evidence.text: Sync fs calls like readFileSync block the event loop until the disk work is done, so no other request is handled meanwhile.
The async or promise versions hand the work off and let the event loop serve other requests while waiting.

notEnough: Only saying use the async version without explaining what the sync one blocks.

misconceptions.text: Says readFileSync inside a request handler is fine because it's fast for small files under any load.

evidence.text: An EventEmitter lets code register listeners with on and trigger them with emit, so parts of the app react to events without calling each other directly.
Each registered listener stays referenced, together with everything its closure holds, until it is removed.
Adding listeners again and again, for example per request, without removing them makes memory grow slowly; Node warns when there are too many listeners.

notEnough: Only saying EventEmitter handles events without explaining how forgotten listeners leak.

groups.title: Module Systems
groups.question: Explain how a Node.js app finds its modules and its configuration.

followUps.CommonJS Module Resolution: How does require find a package, and how can that go wrong in a monorepo?
followUps.Environment Variables & Config: Why should a service validate its environment variables at startup?

evidence.text: require first checks core modules, then relative paths, then walks up through node_modules folders from the current directory.
A module runs once and is cached, so later requires return the same exports.
In a monorepo, packages can resolve to different copies or versions in different node_modules folders, giving duplicate instances or the wrong version.

notEnough: Only saying require loads a file without explaining how it searches.

evidence.text: Configuration like ports, URLs and secrets comes from environment variables, so the same code runs in every environment.
Validating them at startup makes the service stop right away with a clear error instead of failing later with a confusing one.

notEnough: Only saying use environment variables without explaining validation.

groups.title: V8 Engine Internals
groups.question: Explain how the V8 engine affects the speed and memory behavior of a Node.js service.

followUps.V8 JIT Compilation & Hidden Classes: Why does adding object properties in a different order slow down a hot code path?
followUps.Garbage Collection & Memory: How do garbage collection pauses show up in your latency numbers, and how do you keep them short?

evidence.text: V8 compiles hot code into optimized machine code based on the types and object shapes it has seen.
Objects with the same properties added in the same order share a hidden class, which makes property access fast.
Creating objects with different property orders or shapes gives them different hidden classes, so the optimized code is thrown away and the path slows down.

notEnough: Only saying V8 is a JIT compiler without explaining object shapes.

evidence.text: V8 collects new, short-lived objects often and cheaply, and long-lived objects less often in more expensive collections.
Collections can pause JavaScript, which shows up as latency spikes in slow requests.
Creating fewer short-lived objects in hot paths and avoiding a huge long-lived heap keeps pauses short.

notEnough: Only saying JavaScript has garbage collection without explaining how it affects latency.

misconceptions.text: Says memory leaks are impossible in JavaScript because of garbage collection.
